about.title: Stockton Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: A fall is over in a second, but what caused it usually took time to develop. A drink spilled in a grocery aisle and left sitting. A cracked walkway outside an apartment complex in San Joaquin County that nobody patched. A parking lot light out for weeks. Stockton's 305,658 residents move through these spaces every day, along busy corridors like March Lane and Hammer Lane and in the neighborhoods off El Dorado Street and Airport Way. When a property owner knew about a hazard, or reasonably should have, and did nothing to fix it or warn people, California law allows the injured person to seek compensation. That knowledge question, called notice, is where most premises cases are won or lost, which is why what you do in the first days matters. LawProactive is a free service, not a law firm. We connect you with an independent Stockton attorney who handles slip-and-fall and premises claims on contingency, so there is no fee unless your case results in a recovery.

whyChoose.title: Why Stockton Residents Use LawProactive After a Fall

items.title: Notice is the whole case, and we know it
items.desc: In California you generally have to show the owner knew or should have known about the hazard and did nothing. The attorneys we connect you with build that proof early, before cleaning logs and inspection records go missing.

items.title: Surveillance video does not wait
items.desc: Many Stockton stores and complexes overwrite camera footage within days or weeks. Getting a preservation letter out fast can be the difference between your account and hard evidence.

items.title: Deadlines are shorter than people expect
items.desc: California allows two years for most premises claims, but a fall on city, county, or other public property triggers a much shorter government claim window. An attorney can sort out who owns the property and what clock applies.

items.question: I fell on a City of Stockton sidewalk. Is that handled differently than a fall in a store?
items.answer: Yes. When the property belongs to a public entity, such as the City of Stockton, San Joaquin County, or a school district, California requires you to file a formal government claim first, generally within six months of the injury. That is far shorter than the two-year deadline for privately owned property. Because ownership of sidewalks, curbs, and easements is not always obvious, it helps to have an attorney identify the responsible party quickly.

items.question: The store says I should have been watching where I was going. Does that end my claim?
items.answer: Not by itself. California uses pure comparative fault, which means your recovery is reduced by whatever share of blame is assigned to you, but it is not wiped out. If a court decided you were 30 percent responsible for not seeing a spill, you could still recover the remaining 70 percent of your damages. Owners often raise this argument early, and an attorney can push back with photos, witness statements, and the store's own records.

items.question: What should I do right after a fall at a Stockton business or apartment complex?
items.answer: Photograph the hazard from several angles before it is cleaned or repaired, and get names and numbers of anyone who saw it. Ask that an incident report be written and request a copy, and note whether cameras are pointed at the area. Seek medical care the same day, even for pain that seems minor, since fractures and head injuries are often missed at first. Then reach out to us so an attorney can request the footage before it is erased.
